endorsements.quote: Early and continuous engagement of patients and non-academic partners from the conception stage through implementation is essential, as their insights help identify relevant needs, determine where LLMs can be most valuable, and clarify acceptable trade-offs in model selection.
When deemed appropriate, participant compensation must follow guidance from organizations with expertise in patient and public engagement [ 26 , 27 ].

To support meaningful and sustained collaboration with patients and non-academic partners, especially when sensitive or distressing topics may arise, projects must allocate dedicated financial resources and assign clear managerial responsibility (e.g., an engagement coordinator or patient-partnership lead) to oversee communication, ethics, and continuity of participation.
Adopting inclusive governance through multidisciplinary and diverse boards can address ethical considerations, uncover blind spots, and foster inclusive design.

Finally, transparent communication about how AI technologies function—including limitations such as hallucinations and biases—builds trust and empowers users to engage critically with chatbot technology.

General‑purpose LLMs, trained on wide‑ranging clinical and non‑clinical corpora, often lack the domain‑specific nuance that specialised healthcare applications require; therefore, health chatbots must ground their answers in the most current, clinically validated evidence.
We further recommend developing standardized evaluation measures, including PROMs and PREMs, in collaboration with patient and non-academic partners to ensure the relevance of health chatbot trials.

unlisted_practices: Establish data validation committees that include patients and non-academic partners to review and rank data sources for quality and pertinence.
Document AI design and governance decisions transparently through decision logging.
Share real decision-making power with patients and non-academic partners.
Prepare and support engagement participants who may be exposed to distressing material.
Assess patient and partner attitudes toward the increasing use of AI in their care to identify barriers to participation.
Confront power imbalances and avoid tokenistic patient engagement.
Develop educational materials with patient partners about LLM functionalities and limitations to calibrate expectations.

screen.reason: Perspective/commentary outlining recommendations and a framework for patient and non-academic partner engagement in the design, governance, and deployment of LLM health chatbots.
